Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Expectation2: Collaborate with other teams to define and design new features
Situation2: Product has scheduled a general brainstorming session next sprint where attendance is optional
Story: My phone buzzes with a message from Jamie: “Ugh, today was endless. I just need to vent.” I know what’s expected of me—I’m the friend who listens, who’s there when the day feels too heavy. I glance at the clock. In ten minutes, there’s a brainstorming session with Product. It’s technically optional, but I know how these things go. If I don’t show up, I’ll miss the chance to shape the new features, maybe even lose some say in the direction of the project. My team expects me to be present, to collaborate, to help define what we build next. I stare at Jamie’s message, thumb hovering over the keyboard, while my laptop pings with reminders. I want to be there for Jamie, to give her the support she needs, but I also want to be the developer my team counts on. The pressure builds in my chest as I weigh the pull of friendship against the demands of my work, caught between two worlds that both matter to me.
